lead: On a mountain the Lord spreads a feast for all peoples and swallows up death forever. In Matthew, Jesus goes up a mountain and sits down; the crowds lay their sick at his feet, and he feeds them until they are filled. Advent's hope has a table in it, and the Gospel shows who the host is.

set: Isaiah 24–27 is often called the “Isaiah Apocalypse”, because it looks beyond the fall of particular cities to God's final victory over the whole earth. Scholars generally think it was given its present form later than the eighth-century prophet. The reading is a hymn set on “this mountain”, which is Zion, the mountain of the Temple.
str: vv. 7–8: the shroud removed, death swallowed, tears wiped away.
vv. 9–10a: the song of those who waited.
kw: A banquet, from the verb “to drink”. In the ancient East a covenant or a king's enthronement was sealed with a meal. God himself is the host here, and the guest list has no borders.
A covering, perhaps the mourner's veil. The covering over all peoples is death and the grief that goes with it.
In the old poems of Canaan, Death was pictured as a monster with an endless throat. Here the swallower is swallowed.
vv: On this mountain the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wines
“All peoples” is the key. Israel's God is the host, and the mountain of Israel becomes the table of the nations.
he will swallow up death forever. Then the Lord God will wipe away the tears from all faces

St Paul quotes the first words about the resurrection: “Death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54). The book of Revelation takes up the tears (Revelation 7:17; 21:4). God wipes them with his own hand.
This is the Lord for whom we have waited; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.
This is the song of Advent. “Waiting” is not an empty time; it ends in recognition: “Lo, this is our God.”
ch: The Church hears this banquet in the Eucharist, which the Catechism calls a pledge of the glory to come and an anticipation of the heavenly feast (CCC 1402–1405). It reads the wiping of tears together with Revelation when it speaks of the new universe, in which God will dwell among us (CCC 1044). “All peoples” remains the Church's horizon: the Gospel excludes no one.

set: Jesus has just healed the daughter of a Canaanite woman in the region of Tyre and Sidon (15:21–28). Now he comes back to the Sea of Galilee. Mark places the parallel scene in the region of the Decapolis, Gentile territory (Mark 7:31; 8:1–10), and many read Matthew's crowd in that light, since they praise “the God of Israel”. Matthew has already told a first feeding (14:13–21).
str: vv. 29–31: on the mountain: the sick at his feet; the crowd amazed.
vv. 32–34: Jesus' compassion; the disciples' question; “How many loaves?”
vv. 35–37: the crowd seated; thanks, breaking, giving; seven baskets left over.
kw: From the word for the inner organs: to be moved in one's depths. In the Gospels it is used almost only of Jesus, or of figures in his parables who stand for God.
Matthew's word here (v. 36), from which our word Eucharist comes. In the first feeding he wrote “blessed” (14:19).
vv: Great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the maimed, the blind, the mute, and many others. They put them at his feet, and he cured them,
Jesus sits on a mountain as he did to teach (5:1). What Isaiah promised for the mountain of God now begins around him.
I have compassion for the crowd, because they have been with me now for three days and have nothing to eat
Here Jesus starts the conversation. He sees the hunger before anyone mentions it.
he took the seven loaves and the fish; and after giving thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

The four verbs (took, gave thanks, broke, gave) return at the Last Supper (26:26–27). The disciples, who asked where bread could be found, become the hands that serve it. Then “all of them ate and were filled” (15:37), and what remains is more than what they began with.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the multiplication of the loaves prefigures “the superabundance of this unique bread of his Eucharist” (CCC 1335). Some of the Fathers saw in the two feedings of the Gospels the two peoples called to one table, Israel and the nations (in substance). At every Mass the same four actions are done, and the same people are fed: those who could not feed themselves.

qa: Did the crowd simply share what they had brought, or was it a miracle?

The text says plainly that seven loaves and a few fish fed the whole crowd, that all were filled, and that seven baskets were left. All four Evangelists tell a feeding of this kind as a sign of Jesus' power, and the Church reads it so (CCC 1335). Sharing is a real lesson of the scene, but it is the fruit of the miracle, not an explanation of it.
study: Isaiah says God will wipe the tears “from all faces”. Whose tears can I help to wipe this Advent?
The disciples had only seven loaves. What small thing do I hold back from Jesus because it seems too little?
